extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of philosophy/epistemology (general educated audience)
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and tests for judging whether an idea or proposition is genuinely innate (i.e., present in the mind prior to experience), as argued in a philosophical essay against innate principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presence in infancy / early presence in children
rubrics_metrics.description: If an idea is innate it must be 'the first in children, and antecedent to all acquired ones.' (i.e. children should naturally possess it before they acquire other ideas.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test for innateness: ask whether very young children (before relevant experience) have the idea (examples: idea of impossibility or identity). Locke uses rhetorical questions: 'Hath a child an idea of impossibility and identity, before it has of white or black, sweet or bitter?' If not, the idea is unlikely to be innate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universality (universal consent) as proposed evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Proponents claim that universal reception or assent among mankind is evidence that a proposition or idea is innate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke's treatment: while universal consent (or general assent) is offered as proof, he argues that universal reception of the NAME or formulation does not prove the IDEA innate. Example: wide acceptance of the name 'God' does not prove an innate idea of God. He stresses that assent upon hearing (or convention) can produce widespread agreement without innateness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity and distinctness / universal obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: An innate idea should be 'clear and distinct, so as to be universally known and naturally agreed on'; otherwise it cannot be a foundation of universal and undoubted truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke argues that if alleged innate ideas are not clear, distinct, and universally evident, they cannot plausibly be innate. Lack of clarity leads to 'perpetual uncertainty' and refutes the claim of innateness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revival from memory / conscious prior acquaintance
rubrics_metrics.description: Any innate idea must be lodged in memory and therefore revivable with a consciousness that it was perceived before; to remember is to have a consciousness that one knew it previously.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test: when the idea is brought into view, does the person have the consciousness that it was perceived earlier? Locke gives the example of a man who lost sight in childhood and regains it: on regaining sight he gets colour-ideas 'de novo' without consciousness of their having been in his mind before. If alleged innate ideas cannot be so remembered, they are not in the mind prior to experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation-ideas require their base ideas to be innate
rubrics_metrics.description: If a relational idea (e.g. WHOLE and PART) were innate, then the positive ideas on which that relation depends (e.g. extension and number) must themselves be innate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Logical entailment test: you cannot have an innate idea of a relation without also having innate ideas of the relata. Locke uses this to argue that whole/part cannot be innate because extension and number are not innate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-cultural and historical absence undermines innateness
rubrics_metrics.description: If whole peoples or nations lack a notion (e.g. of God), that absence is evidence against the idea being innate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke cites reports of nations with no notion or name for God (examples from voyages to Soldania, Brazil, the Caribbees) to show that the idea of God is not universal and therefore unlikely to be innate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Having a name does not imply innate idea
rubrics_metrics.description: The mere existence of a common name in a language (for fire, sun, God, etc.) does not prove the corresponding idea is innate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke: words can spread ideas by communication; the presence of a word or name among many people is often due to cultural transmission, not an original imprint on the mind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variety or contradiction of concepts under one name
rubrics_metrics.description: If people under the same name have contrary or inconsistent ideas (e.g. differing, even opposing, conceptions of 'God'), that disagreement indicates the idea is not innately imprinted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke: agreeing in a name but disagreeing in concept shows the name came from language and convention rather than a single innate impression. Example: wide variance in ideas of God under the same name within a country.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gross, ignorant, or crude conceptions argue against innateness
rubrics_metrics.description: Widespread crude or anthropomorphic conceptions (e.g. many deities, corporeal images) are inconsistent with the claim that a true idea of God was innately imprinted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke's point: if true innate impressions existed, we would not find the vulgar holding low, pitiful, or contradictory notions of the object in question; the prevalence of such crude notions counts against innateness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Innateness would make principles distinguishable from acquired truths
rubrics_metrics.description: If there were innate ideas, they would be plainly different from other acquired perceptions and every person would find them true in himself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke challenges advocates to name such distinct innate impressions; absence of such unmistakable, self-evident impressions argues that no such innate ideas exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical usefulness and certainty as a test
rubrics_metrics.description: It would be odd for God to imprint on minds principles that are of little use or little certainty; innate principles should be useful and evident.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke argues that supposed innate speculative principles are of little use and practical ones are not self-evident; this mismatch weakens the claim that such principles were divinely imprinted. He invites proponents to identify which principles are so useful and clear as to demand innateness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right use of natural faculties can generate the knowledge (no need for innateness)
rubrics_metrics.description: If human faculties (sensation, reflection, reasoning) suffice to discover the idea, there is no need to posit an innate impression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke's positive account: many general ideas result from proper application of faculties to experience (examples: discovery of God via reflection on creation; mathematical truths via reasoning). The ability of faculties to produce the idea undermines claims of innateness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence by immediate assent upon hearing is not proof of innateness
rubrics_metrics.description: Assenting to a proposition when hearing it (or taking it on trust) does not prove the underlying ideas are innate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke compares this to a blind man hearing that saffron is yellow and assenting when sight is restored: assent on hearing or after being told can follow from acquiring the ideas, not from prior innate possession of them.

rubrics_metrics.name: If innate, the idea should be uniformly apparent across those of mature judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: Advocates sometimes claim that wise or thoughtful men everywhere attain certain true notions (e.g. of God), but if these are the product of thought rather than imprint, their presence among the wise does not prove innateness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke distinguishes between the limited universality among 'wise men' (few in number) and true innateness; he argues that wise men's agreement more plausibly shows the power of proper reflection than an original imprint.
